title: International Consensus on Physical Exercise. How Do I Interpret the Clinical Guidelines?
summary:
This chapter compares the main international guidelines on exercise in pregnancy: WHO, ACOG, CSEP/SOGC, RCOG, RANZCOG and SEGO. Research over the past 50 years offers a reassuring margin of safety, and the guidelines agree that regular, safe exercise is part of prenatal care. They differ in terminology, risk classification, recommended intensity and level of evidence, so knowing those differences helps apply them in context.

All guidelines recommend at least 150 min of moderate-intensity activity per week, spread over several days, built on aerobic and muscle-strengthening work. They agree on absolute and relative contraindications, avoiding prolonged supine positions after week 20, and avoiding falls or abdominal trauma. Differences reflect method, local culture and clinical emphasis rather than contradiction. The chapter also lists limits, such as little evidence on high-intensity exercise in high-risk pregnancies, and treats guidelines as a flexible framework.
points: Healthy pregnant women are advised to do 150 min of moderate physical activity at least 3 days a week, ideally with professional supervision.
WHO allows 150 min of moderate-intensity or 75 min of high-intensity activity per week, and advises avoiding prolonged inactivity.
ACOG advises avoiding supine exercise after the 20th week, hot and humid environments, and activities with a risk of falling or abdominal trauma.
CSEP/SOGC, RCOG, RANZCOG and SEGO all recommend at least 150 min of moderate-intensity activity per week, spread through the week.
Vigorous intensity is allowed by RCOG and RANZCOG only if the woman was previously active; RCOG is more conservative than ACOG.
Priority goes to aerobic activities (walking, swimming, stationary cycling) and core and lower-body strengthening, supplemented by flexibility work.

Absolute contraindications include cervical incompetence, placenta praevia with active bleeding and uncontrolled preeclampsia; relative ones include multiple pregnancy and maternal cardiovascular disease.
Documented benefits include gestational weight control, lower risk of gestational diabetes and preeclampsia, better mental health, less musculoskeletal pain and preparation for childbirth.
Known limitations include limited evidence on high-intensity exercise in high-risk pregnancies and limited long-term data on infant neurocognitive and metabolic development.
takeaways: Aim for at least 150 min of moderate activity per week, spread across several days.
Check the guidelines of your own country or region for local particularities.
Adapt the plan to your activity history, health status, obstetric conditions and preferences.
Use the Borg or a similar perceived exertion scale to set intensity.
Involve obstetricians, physiotherapists and certified trainers, especially for supervised programs.
When reading a guideline, check the level of evidence and whether a rule is absolute or relative.
cautions: Avoid exercising on your back for long periods after week 20.
Avoid hot and humid environments and activities with a risk of falling or abdominal trauma.
Stop exercising and seek care if warning signs appear, such as bleeding, pain, contractions or dizziness.
